newsitem.title: USA: Democrat wins primary for Wash. state governor.
newsitem.headline: Democrat wins primary for Wash. state governor.

text.p: King County executive Gary Locke won the race for Democratic nominee for Washington state governor while the top two Republican candidates were so close officials Wednesday were unable to call a winner.
In claiming victory, Locke said he would be a consensus builder. "The people are tired of partisan gridlock," he said.

With 97 percent of precincts reporting, Locke, the elected administrator for the county that includes Seattle, had 192,886 votes, or 24 percent of the total in the state's open primary system, compared with 146,705 or 18 percent for Seattle Mayor Norm Rice, his closest challenger.

Among Republicans, former state Sen. Ellen Craswell had 15 percent of the vote against 14 percent for state House Majority leader Dale Foreman. The race was expected to be decided by absentee votes, which could take days to count.
A total of 15 candidates ran in the primary for the chance to succeed Democratic Gov. Mike Lowry, who is stepping down after one term marred by a sexual harassment scandal.

While cautioning that up to a third of the state's votes could be cast by absentee ballot, Locke was confident and stopped just short of declaring victory at a raucous party in a Seattle microbrewery late Tuesday.
"The way things are going, we can start celebrating," he said.

Locke, 46, served 11 years in the state House before taking on the high-profile King County job. He is the son of Chinese immigrants and would be the nation's first Asian-American governor outside Hawaii.

Craswell, 64, a former medical technician, comes from the powerful Christian conservative wing of the state's Republican Party, while Foreman, 48, is an attorney and fruit farmer who is considered more moderate.

The primary came just a day before a Seattle campaign stop by President Clinton, who is favoured to win Washington state as he did in 1992. Clinton and the Democrats are hoping to reverse the GOP's big gains of 1994, when six of the state's nine House seats changed to Republican hands.
While no incumbents faced challenges within their own party, several Republican freshmen were considered vulnerable in November.
In eastern Washington's Fifth District, wheat farmer Judy Olson won the right to challenge Republican Representative George Nethercutt, who unseated House Speaker Thomas Foley in 1994.
State Sen. Kevin Quigley got the nod to challenge freshman Republican Representative Jack Metcalf in the Second District in the northwest part of the state.
In central Washington's Fourth District Rick Locke was the leading Democrat in the race to challenge Representative Doc Hastings.

In the First District, which includes Seattle's northeastern suburbs, in a race also too close to call Democrats Jeff Coopersmith and Don Stuart were vying for the right to challenge Representative Rick White.
